query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: The degradation of additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases is governed by the selective oxidation or reduction of specific elements (e.g., Al or Ti) at grain boundaries, leading to embrittlement and potential catastrophic failure.
generation.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled variation in the alloy composition by reducing the Al content by 50% while maintaining the fcc matrix structure.
generation.conditions: Elevated-temperature exposure (e.g., 800°C) to oxidizing (e.g., O2) or reducing (e.g., H2) gas environments for 100 hours.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundary chemistry and the formation of brittle oxide or reduced phases.
generation.mechanism: The selective oxidation or reduction of Al or Ti at grain boundaries creates brittle phases that compromise the mechanical integrity of the alloy, leading to crack initiation and propagation under thermal or mechanical stress.
generation.predicted_outcome: Reducing the Al content will decrease the formation of brittle oxide phases at grain boundaries, resulting in improved resistance to embrittlement and a lower likelihood of catastrophic failure compared to the baseline alloy.
generation.baseline: Degradation behavior of the original Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy under identical conditions.
generation.boundary: Applicable to temperatures up to 1000°C and gas environments with partial pressures of oxidizing or reducing species typical of industrial processes.
generation.uncertainty: Limited understanding of the exact role of Al and Ti in grain boundary chemistry and their interaction with oxidizing or reducing gases.

falsification_experiment.design: Expose both the original and modified alloys to oxidizing and reducing gas environments at 800°C for 100 hours, followed by mechanical testing (e.g., tensile or fracture toughness tests) and microstructural analysis (e.g., SEM, EDS, TEM) to assess grain boundary integrity and phase formation.
measurements: Mechanical properties (e.g., tensile strength, fracture toughness)
Grain boundary composition and phase identification
Extent of oxidation or reduction at grain boundaries
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified alloy with reduced Al content exhibits similar or worse embrittlement and mechanical degradation compared to the baseline alloy, the hypothesis that selective oxidation or reduction of Al governs degradation is falsified.
